nodes.title: Conditional Access: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Conditional Access is the Entra ID policy engine that decides, per sign-in, whether to allow, block, or add requirements based on signals like user, device, location, and risk. It's the core of Zero Trust enforcement in the Microsoft cloud.

flashcards.front: How does a Conditional Access policy work?
flashcards.back: It's if-then: assignments (users/groups, target apps, conditions like location/device/risk) define WHEN it applies; access controls define WHAT happens — block, or grant with requirements (MFA, compliant device, approved app). Policies evaluate at every sign-in.

Require multi-factor authentication, require a compliant or hybrid-joined device, require an approved client app or app protection policy, and require terms of use. Multiple controls can be combined with AND/OR.

It evaluates a policy and logs what WOULD have happened without enforcing it — so you can validate impact before turning a policy on. Essential for avoiding accidental lockouts when rolling out new policies.

flashcards.front: How does risk feed into Conditional Access?
flashcards.back: Entra ID Protection scores sign-in risk (impossible travel, anonymous IP) and user risk (leaked credentials). Conditional Access can require MFA on medium risk or block/force a secure password change on high risk — automated, signal-driven response.

questions.q: An organization adopting Zero Trust must enforce explicit verification on every workload request, regardless of the source network. Which architectural pattern most directly implements the verify-explicitly pillar across Microsoft Entra workloads?
choices: Place all corporate workloads behind a single perimeter VPN that authenticates users once at tunnel establishment and treats every flow inside the tunnel as trusted for the session
Require Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies that evaluate user, device compliance, location, application, and real-time risk signals on every sign-in to every workload
Issue long-lived service principal client secrets to every application identity and rotate them on a 90-day schedule through an Azure Key Vault rotation policy
Apply the Entra security defaults baseline tenant-wide so that MFA is enforced on administrative roles only and standard user sign-ins are unchallenged
questions.explanation: Verify-explicitly requires authenticating and authorizing every request using all available signals — identity, device posture, location, application, and real-time risk. Entra Conditional Access is the policy engine that evaluates those signals at every sign-in. A perimeter VPN trusts whatever sits behind it once the tunnel is up — the opposite of Zero Trust. Long-lived secrets, even rotated quarterly, still embed implicit trust between rotations and do not evaluate per-request signals. Security defaults are a minimal MFA baseline; they do not implement signal-driven per-request authorization across the tenant.

questions.q: An architect is designing privileged access for Azure subscriptions under Zero Trust. Administrators must hold no standing high-privilege roles; instead, elevated access should be requested just in time, time-bound, and require approval and MFA. Which Microsoft capability should anchor this design?
choices: Assign administrators permanent Owner roles at subscription scope but require a Conditional Access policy enforcing MFA at every sign-in for those accounts
Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management with eligible role assignments that require activation with approval, MFA, and an expiration time
Place all administrators into a single security group and grant the group the Owner role at the management-group scope to simplify operational handoff
Issue each administrator a separate break-glass account with a standing Global Administrator role stored in a vaulted credential record
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management (PIM) makes roles eligible rather than permanent, so administrators activate access just in time with approval, MFA, and an expiry — eliminating standing privilege per Zero Trust. Permanent Owner roles with MFA still leave standing high privilege available at all times; a stolen session bypasses MFA after sign-in. A group with permanent Owner at management-group scope broadens standing access further. Break-glass accounts are emergency-only with strict monitoring; they are not the model for routine administration and don't satisfy the just-in-time requirement.

questions.q: A Zero Trust network strategy for Azure PaaS data services must ensure that traffic from application subnets to Azure Storage and Azure SQL never traverses the public internet and that the services are not reachable from public endpoints. Which design satisfies both goals?
choices: Enable service endpoints on the application subnets and keep the storage and SQL public endpoints enabled to preserve compatibility with management tooling
Deploy Azure Private Endpoints for the storage and SQL resources inside the application VNet subnets and disable public network access on both services entirely
Restrict the storage and SQL resource firewalls to the application subnet's public outbound NAT IP ranges and otherwise leave the services internet-reachable
Route all outbound application traffic through an Azure NAT gateway so the source IP is stable and allow-listed in the storage and SQL service firewalls
questions.explanation: Private Endpoints give the PaaS services private IPs inside the VNet so traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone, and disabling public network access removes the public endpoint entirely — satisfying both requirements. Service endpoints keep the public endpoint reachable and route over Azure's network but do not provide a private IP or remove public exposure. Firewalling to outbound public IPs still uses the public endpoint and exposes it to whatever can spoof or reach those addresses. A NAT gateway only stabilizes the source IP; the services remain publicly addressable.

questions.q: Threat modeling for a payment microservice running on Azure Kubernetes Service must ensure that a compromised pod cannot reach secrets or other namespaces, and that container images are verified before deployment. Which combination best reflects a Zero Trust workload design?
choices: Grant the AKS cluster a single highly privileged service account shared across all workload pods and store secrets as plain Kubernetes generic Secret resources with no envelope encryption
Use Kubernetes network policies and per-workload managed identities with Microsoft Defender for Containers and image scanning that gates deployment of unverified images
Disable Kubernetes network policies to simplify pod-to-pod communication and rely on a perimeter Azure Firewall to block lateral movement inside the cluster
Run all workloads in the default namespace with a permissive pod security context so the platform team has a single consolidated place to apply controls
questions.explanation: Kubernetes network policies segment pod-to-pod and namespace traffic, per-workload managed identities give each pod least-privilege access to Azure resources, and Defender for Containers with image scanning blocks unverified images before deployment — a layered Zero Trust workload design. A single shared privileged service account plus generic secrets maximizes blast radius if any pod is compromised. Disabling network policies removes in-cluster segmentation; a perimeter Azure Firewall cannot inspect east-west traffic between pods on the same node. Running everything in the default namespace with permissive security contexts removes isolation rather than centralizing controls.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A CISO wants to consolidate three legacy SIEM products and reduce mean time to respond across endpoint, identity, email, and cloud telemetry. Which Microsoft pattern best satisfies a converged SOC strategy?
choices: Configure Microsoft Sentinel as the sole incident destination with Defender XDR's native incident creation disabled, so every Defender XDR detection flows into Sentinel for triage instead of remaining in the Defender portal
Use Microsoft Defender XDR only, since the unified Defender portal handles incidents, hunting, and automation across Microsoft products and removes the need for a separate SIEM
Keep all three existing SIEMs in parallel, forward Defender XDR alerts to each through the Microsoft Graph Security API, and build a custom correlation layer to deduplicate cases
Use Microsoft Defender XDR for native correlation across endpoints, identities, email, and apps, and use Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM for remaining log sources and case management
questions.explanation: Microsoft's reference SOC architecture pairs Defender XDR (native cross-product correlation for endpoints, identities, email, and apps) with Sentinel as the SIEM/SOAR for additional log sources, long-term retention, and case management. Disabling XDR's incident creation and routing raw detections into Sentinel breaks native correlation and duplicates triage. Defender XDR alone cannot ingest arbitrary non-Microsoft telemetry. Running three SIEMs in parallel with a custom dedup layer preserves the silos the consolidation was meant to remove and adds brittle glue code.

questions.q: An organization wants threat intelligence and detection rules to be evaluated against the MITRE ATT&CK framework so the SOC can identify coverage gaps across tactics and techniques. Which design best provides ATT&CK-aligned coverage visibility within the Microsoft stack?
choices: Export all Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules to a third-party spreadsheet and manually tag each rule with an ATT&CK technique ID on a quarterly review cadence
Rely on Microsoft Defender XDR alert titles alone and map each to a tactic by reading the alert description during incident triage
Use the Microsoft Sentinel MITRE ATT&CK coverage view to map active analytics rules and hunting queries to tactics and techniques and reveal coverage gaps
Assign an Azure Policy initiative that audits whether each subscription has at least one analytics rule enabled, regardless of which technique the rule detects
questions.explanation: Microsoft Sentinel includes a built-in MITRE ATT&CK coverage view that maps active analytics rules and hunting queries onto the ATT&CK matrix, directly revealing which tactics and techniques are covered or missing. Manually tagging rules in a spreadsheet is error-prone and stale by the next sprint. Reading Defender XDR alert titles during triage gives ad-hoc per-incident context, not systematic framework-wide coverage. An Azure Policy audit of whether any rule exists per subscription says nothing about technique-level coverage and only checks subscription configuration.

questions.q: An organization in scope of PCI DSS and HIPAA needs a single view of control coverage across Azure and AWS that maps each control to both frameworks. Which Microsoft service should anchor the design?
choices: Microsoft Sentinel content hub solutions for PCI DSS and HIPAA, deployed against a workspace that ingests AWS CloudTrail events through the Amazon Web Services data connector
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager assessments with the PCI DSS and HIPAA templates, scored against the in-scope Microsoft 365 tenant and surfaced through the Purview compliance portal
Microsoft Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance dashboard with the PCI DSS and HIPAA/HITRUST standards added to the AWS connector and to the Azure subscriptions in scope
Azure Policy regulatory compliance built-in initiative assignments at Azure management groups, replicated as service control policies inside the AWS organization through a synchronization script
questions.explanation: Defender for Cloud's regulatory compliance dashboard evaluates Azure and AWS resources against PCI DSS, HIPAA/HITRUST, ISO 27001, NIST and other standards through a single pane with control-to-framework mapping. Sentinel solutions deliver detections and workbooks, not control-coverage scoring. Purview Compliance Manager scores Microsoft 365 and Azure tenant controls; it does not assess AWS workload configuration. Azure Policy applies to Azure resources, and reproducing controls as AWS service control policies via scripting is brittle and does not produce framework-mapped scoring across both clouds.

questions.q: A new Azure landing zone must continuously evaluate posture against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark and apply preventive guardrails at the management-group scope. Which combination achieves this with the least drift?
choices: Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud on each individual subscription as it is created and assign MCSB per subscription, so each subscription owner controls its own posture configuration

Package MCSB and the additional policy guardrails together using Azure Blueprints assigned at every subscription, accepting that blueprints are now deprecated but still functional during the transition
Use Microsoft Sentinel analytics rules to detect deviations from MCSB and trigger Logic Apps playbooks that remediate drift after the fact at the resource level inside each subscription
Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud at the root management group with MCSB assigned as the default standard and Azure Policy initiatives deployed at management-group scope as guardrails
questions.explanation: Enabling Defender for Cloud at the root management group inherits MCSB to every subscription beneath it — including future ones — and Azure Policy initiatives at management-group scope apply preventive guardrails (deny/audit/deployIfNotExists) without per-subscription drift. Per-subscription enablement requires continuous reconciliation and misses subscriptions added later. Azure Blueprints are deprecated and Microsoft's published guidance is to move to policy at management-group scope instead. Sentinel + playbooks react after a deviation has already occurred — detection, not prevention.

questions.q: External partners must access a curated set of internal applications using credentials from their existing Microsoft Entra tenants, without you provisioning shadow accounts. Which design satisfies the requirement with the least overhead?
choices: Configure Microsoft Entra cross-tenant access and B2B collaboration so partner guests authenticate from their home tenant and are governed through entitlement management access packages
Stand up an Active Directory Federation Services farm in the perimeter and configure a SAML federation trust with each partner's identity provider for inbound authentication brokering
Synchronize each partner's directory into your tenant with Microsoft Entra Connect cloud sync so partner users appear as fully provisioned member accounts inside your own tenant
Issue every partner an internal Microsoft Entra member account, enforce MFA on it, and rotate the credential every 30 days through a documented help-desk process
questions.explanation: Cross-tenant access settings plus B2B collaboration let partner identities authenticate against their own home tenant while you authorize them as guests, with entitlement management automating access reviews and lifecycle. An ADFS federation farm requires per-partner trust configuration, certificate maintenance, and a perimeter server footprint — high operational burden vs. cross-tenant access. Connect cloud sync of a partner directory turns external users into member identities inside your tenant, defeating the no-shadow-account requirement. Issuing and rotating internal accounts is literally the shadow-account pattern the requirement forbids.

questions.q: Hybrid Windows and Linux servers spread across Azure, AWS, and on-premises must receive EDR, vulnerability assessment, and file integrity monitoring through one control plane. Which design meets the requirement?
choices: Onboard non-Azure servers through Azure Arc, then enable Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 2 on the connected subscriptions to deliver EDR, vulnerability assessment, and FIM uniformly
Install Microsoft Defender for Endpoint directly on every server without Azure Arc and rely on the Defender for Endpoint portal alone to deliver EDR, vulnerability assessment, and FIM
Forward Windows event logs and Linux syslog to Microsoft Sentinel and build custom KQL analytics rules to approximate EDR detections, vulnerability findings, and file integrity changes
Deploy the Microsoft Monitoring Agent on every server reporting into a Log Analytics workspace and use Update Management plus Change Tracking to cover vulnerability and integrity needs
questions.explanation: Azure Arc projects non-Azure servers into Azure Resource Manager so that subscription-scoped Defender for Servers Plan 2 can deliver Defender for Endpoint EDR, integrated vulnerability assessment (Defender Vulnerability Management), and file integrity monitoring under one control plane. MDE alone delivers EDR but does not surface the host through Azure posture management and leaves vulnerability assessment and FIM as separate point products. Sentinel KQL approximations are detective only and miss kernel-level EDR signals. MMA + Update Management + Change Tracking does not provide EDR and does not perform true file integrity monitoring.

questions.q: A hub-and-spoke topology must inspect all spoke-to-spoke traffic and all outbound internet traffic, including TLS inspection on egress. Which strategy delivers this with the least operational burden?
choices: Apply a deny-by-default network security group on every spoke subnet with explicit allow rules for required east-west flows, and enable NSG flow logs for traffic analytics
Deploy Azure Application Gateway with Web Application Firewall in the hub and route all spoke-to-spoke and outbound internet traffic through Application Gateway listeners and backend pools
Deploy Azure Firewall Premium in the hub virtual network, force spoke-to-spoke and outbound traffic through it via user-defined routes, and enable TLS inspection on Azure Firewall Premium
Peer every spoke virtual network directly to every other spoke in a full mesh and apply NSG rules at each subnet to enforce east-west segmentation between application workloads
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall Premium in the hub, combined with UDRs that funnel spoke and outbound traffic to it, performs stateful inspection and adds TLS inspection and IDPS without per-spoke configuration. NSGs filter at L3/L4 only and cannot perform deep-packet or TLS inspection. Application Gateway is a reverse proxy for HTTP(S) inbound web workloads, not a general-purpose egress and inter-VNet inspection device. A full spoke-to-spoke mesh sidesteps central inspection entirely and scales as O(n²) peerings, increasing operational burden as the landing zone grows.

questions.q: A CISO needs visibility into shadow IT use, session controls on sanctioned SaaS applications, and data loss prevention on third-party cloud storage. Which design anchors the SaaS security strategy?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 with Safe Links, Safe Attachments, and attack simulation training extended to cover phishing scenarios that target SaaS sign-in pages
Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention policies extended across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams, with Endpoint DLP enrolled on managed devices to control how files leave the tenant
Microsoft Sentinel data connectors for each individual SaaS vendor, with analytics rules that detect anomalous activity and Logic Apps playbooks that revoke user sessions after each detection
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps with cloud discovery from firewall logs, Conditional Access app control for session policies, and file policies on connected third-party SaaS storage providers
questions.explanation: Defender for Cloud Apps is Microsoft's SaaS security control plane: cloud discovery surfaces shadow IT from firewall/proxy logs, Conditional Access app control routes sessions through a reverse proxy to enforce session policies, and connected app file policies apply DLP across third-party cloud storage. Defender for Office 365 protects mail and Office collaboration — it does not discover shadow SaaS or enforce inline session controls. Purview DLP covers Microsoft 365 workloads and managed endpoints; it does not discover unsanctioned SaaS or apply inline session policies to third-party apps. Sentinel ingests SaaS logs for detection but cannot enforce inline session controls or perform real-time cloud discovery.
